nameStory: The Bicolored Sallow gets its name from its distinctive two-toned appearance, with contrasting light and dark patches on its wings. 'Sallow' comes from an old English word meaning 'pale' or 'yellowish,' referring to the moth's typically muted, earthy colors that help it blend with tree bark and dried leaves.
description: The Bicolored Sallow is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1.5 inches that's active during fall and early winter. Its forewings display a striking pattern of cream, brown, and gray patches that create a marbled or mottled appearance. Like other moths in the cutworm family, it has a sturdy, somewhat fuzzy body and holds its wings tent-like over its back when at rest. This hardy moth can be found flying on surprisingly cool autumn nights when most other moths have finished their season.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Forewings show distinct light cream or pale yellow patches contrasting with darker brown or gray areas, creating a patchwork quilt effect that feels slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan around 1.5 inches and a robust, hairy body that appears stocky compared to more delicate moths

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: When resting, holds wings in a steep tent-like position over the body, rather than spread flat like many other moth species

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are slightly thicker in males, lacking the feathery appearance of some other fall moths

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Flies with a steady, somewhat heavy flight pattern and is attracted to lights on cool autumn evenings

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Dense, soft fuzzy covering on the thorax and abdomen that helps insulate against cool weather

habitat: Bicolored Sallows inhabit mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly areas with oak, maple, and other hardwood trees. They prefer woodland edges, clearings, and suburban areas with mature trees, from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains. The moths are often found near deciduous trees where their caterpillars feed on various hardwood species.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active; eggs laid the previous fall begin hatching into tiny caterpillars that will feed on emerging tree buds and young leaves.
seasonality.summer: Caterpillars continue developing through the summer months, feeding on deciduous tree foliage before pupating in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak flight season occurs from September through November, when adults emerge and can be seen at lights on cool evenings, even after first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults may occasionally fly on unusually warm winter nights in southern New England, but most activity ceases until the following fall.

funFact: Bicolored Sallows are among the few moths that actually seem to enjoy cold weather, often flying actively on frosty October nights when temperatures drop into the 30s – conditions that would ground most other moth species!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other sallow moths, but the Bicolored Sallow's distinct two-toned wing pattern sets it apart from the more uniformly colored species. Remember: if it looks like someone took a paintbrush and dabbed light patches on a brown moth, you've likely found a Bicolored Sallow.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'sallow' in moth names refers to their generally pale, muted coloration and shouldn't be confused with sallow trees (a type of willow), though both share the same etymological root meaning 'pale' or 'grayish.'
compareHints: As the only Sunira species commonly found in New England, the Bicolored Sallow is most similar to other sallow moths in the Noctuidae family. However, it can be distinguished from related species like the Satellite moth or various Xanthia sallows by its distinctive two-toned wing pattern and later flight period extending well into winter.
